The rule to be used is the one given in the chapter. While travelling from the west of the IDL to its east, the existing day and date are kept even after crossing the line, so the date on the eastern side stays one day behind. While travelling from the east of the IDL to its west, one day has to be added.

(A) The arrow runs from the 150° E box towards the 150° W box, so the journey is from the west of the IDL to its east. The day and date must therefore not be moved ahead; the day already spent has to be counted again. Monday, 15th August at 150° E becomes Sunday, 14th August at 150° W.

(B) The arrow runs from the 170° W box towards the 80° E box, so the journey is from the east of the IDL to its west. Here one day has to be added. Sunday, 25th December at 170° W becomes Monday, 26th December at 80° E.

|---|---|---|
| (A) | 150° E, Monday, 15th August | 150° W — Sunday, 14th August |
| (B) | 170° W, Sunday, 25th December | 80° E — Monday, 26th December |

The IDL brings coordination between international airlines, transportation services, and economic and trade activities. It was carved out of the necessity of coordinating time and date, and that necessity is far greater in today's modern era of rapidly happening global developments. With the help of the IDL, all the calculations of day and time can be kept track of accurately in global transportation, especially with respect to airways. It is only because of the IDL that the schedules of traffic worldwide are organised properly. For all these reasons the IDL is proving to be very useful in today's times.

With reference to the IDL, the day on the earth starts in the west of the line and ends in its east. An attempt has been made to make the IDL pass through the Pacific Ocean completely, so this changeover from one date to the next takes place in the middle of that ocean. It is one and the same day only at 12 o'clock midnight at the 180° meridian; immediately to the west of the line, in countries such as Japan and Australia, a new day begins, while to the east of it, in countries such as the USA and Chile, the day is ending. Since the line along which a new day begins lies in the Pacific Ocean, the day on the earth starts in the Pacific Ocean.

Two points were taken into consideration while drawing the International Date Line: the direction of travel, and the current day and date. The line was drawn opposite to the Greenwich Prime Meridian, that is, with reference to the 180° meridian, because by convention the start and the end of a date is considered to be at that meridian. Care was also taken to make the line pass through the Pacific Ocean completely, so that it would not cut across land or islands; for this reason it turns east at some places and west at others instead of running straight. The decision was taken by representatives of many nations who got together under the leadership of the American professor Davidson in the year 1884. The line has been changed as and when required, the last change being made in 2011, but its maximum part still coincides with the 180° meridian.

The change to be made depends on the direction of travel and on the current day and date. If I travel from the west of the IDL to its east, as from Japan to America, I will keep the existing day and date even after crossing the line; if it is Thursday, 25th December before crossing, I will still consider it Thursday, 25th December. If I travel from the east of the IDL to its west, as from America to Japan, I will add one day; Thursday, 25th December will then become Friday, 26th December. Changing the day and the date in this way while crossing the line is an international convention, and it is what keeps the calculations of day and time correct for the rest of the journey.

An attempt has been made to make the IDL pass through the Pacific Ocean completely. Had it been drawn perfectly straight along the 180° meridian, it would have passed through land and some islands. The people living there would then have had to follow different dates and timings, because the dates would have been different on the eastern and the western parts of their own land. It would also have been difficult to know exactly when one crosses the line on land and when the date changes on the calendar. To avoid this, the line was bent — at places it turns east and at other places it turns west — although its maximum part still coincides with the 180° meridian.

The IDL is the line at which the day and the date change. If it passed through land, the eastern part and the western part of that land would have had different dates at the same moment, and the people living there would have had to follow different dates and timings. It would also have been difficult for a traveller to know when the line had been crossed on land and when the date had to be changed on the calendar. To avoid this confusion, an attempt has been made to make the IDL pass through the Pacific Ocean completely, the line turning east or west wherever land or islands come in its way.

The 180° meridian lies exactly opposite to the Greenwich Prime Meridian. Whether one goes east or west from the Prime Meridian, the 180° meridian is reached after 12 hours, so it is the fitting place at which a date should begin and end. According to the convention, the start and the end of a date is therefore considered to be at the 180° meridian. When representatives of many nations decided upon the International Date Line in 1884, they drew it opposite to the Greenwich Prime Meridian, that is, with reference to the 180° meridian. Even though the line bends here and there so as to stay in the Pacific Ocean, its maximum part still coincides with the 180° meridian, and so the IDL is considered with respect to that meridian only.

Yes. The IDL will be crossed once, on the last leg of the route, from Los Angeles to Tokyo. Mumbai, London, New York and Los Angeles are all reached by travelling westward across the Greenwich Prime Meridian, and none of these legs comes anywhere near the 180° meridian. The journey from Los Angeles to Tokyo, however, goes across the Pacific Ocean, and it is through this ocean that the IDL passes. Los Angeles lies to the east of the IDL, while Tokyo, being in Japan, lies to its west, so the line is crossed from its east to its west and one day will have to be added. On the map, mark the crossing on the Los Angeles–Tokyo leg.

No. The IDL will not be crossed on this route. Delhi, Kolkata, Singapore and Melbourne all lie on the eastern meridians, that is, on the western side of the IDL. The route runs eastward and then southward, but it stops well short of the 180° meridian along which the IDL runs, and it does not enter that part of the Pacific Ocean through which the line passes. As the line is never reached, no change of day or date has to be made anywhere on this journey.

Yes. The IDL will be crossed once, on the last leg of the route, from Tokyo to San Francisco. Kolkata, Hong Kong and Tokyo all lie on the eastern meridians, that is, on the western side of the IDL, so no crossing takes place among them. The journey from Tokyo to San Francisco crosses the Pacific Ocean, through which the IDL passes, and San Francisco lies to the east of the line. As the crossing is from the west of the line to its east, the existing day and date are kept even after crossing, so the date does not move ahead. The plane that left Shanghai on 1st January 2017 and reached San Francisco on 31st December 2016 shows this reverse change of date. Mark the crossing on the Tokyo–San Francisco leg on the map.

Yes. The IDL will be crossed once, on the last leg of the route, from Sydney to Santiago. Chennai, Singapore, Tokyo and Sydney all lie on the eastern meridians, that is, on the western side of the IDL — Japan and Australia are among the countries that lie to the west of the line. The journey from Sydney to Santiago crosses the Pacific Ocean, through which the IDL passes, and Santiago is in Chile, a country lying to the east of the line. So the line is crossed from its west to its east, and the existing day and date have to be kept even after crossing. Mark the crossing on the Sydney–Santiago leg on the map.

No. The IDL will not be crossed on this route. The journey runs westward all the way, from Delhi to London and then onward to New York, so the meridian it crosses is the Greenwich Prime Meridian and not the 180° meridian. New York does lie on the western meridians, but it is still far to the east of the IDL, which passes through the Pacific Ocean on the far side of the earth from this route. Since the route never reaches the Pacific Ocean or the 180° meridian, there is no change of day or date to be made on this journey.
